posts.title: Why rolling over in bed can set off a spin
posts.excerpt: A short burst of spinning when you roll over in bed is a common reason people book the 60-minute first assessment at Taira Clinic.
posts.content:
You turn onto your side and the room turns with you. You grip the sheet and wait for it to settle. Some people sit up and find the same spin when they lie back down. Others feel steady once they are still, then lose the room again the next time they look up to a high shelf. At Taira Clinic this is one of the histories we hear most at the desk. It is also why a positional test sits inside the first assessment, rather than a set of exercises chosen from the phone call alone.

The pattern has a name you may already have heard: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, shortened to BPPV. In plain terms, small crystals that belong in one part of the inner ear have drifted into a canal that senses turning. When you roll over, those crystals shift, the canal reports a rotation that is not happening, and the eyes flick as if the room were moving. The gaze chart on our wall is dots and arrows, not letters, so we can watch that eye movement without asking you to read. Video goggles do the same job in the chair. The positional test then places you in the positions that set the spin off, including rolling and tipping back, so we can see which canal is involved.

A spin in bed is not always BPPV. Vestibular neuritis tends to arrive as a longer, harder attack, with nausea and with unsteadiness that remains after the violent spinning eases. Ménière's-type episodes often bring ear fullness, a change in hearing, or a noise in the ear, and they come back. Vestibular migraine can produce motion sensitivity with or without a headache. A head knock can leave post-concussion dizziness that is not a crystal problem. Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness is different again: an ongoing sway or fog, worse upright, worse in a busy station or a bright aisle. If screens and supermarket aisles are the trigger, the plan looks more like graded visual exposure than a single repositioning manoeuvre. The point of the 60-minute first assessment is to sort these pictures instead of guessing from the bedroom story.

When the positional test fits BPPV, the next visit is often a repositioning visit. That visit is 30 minutes and the fee is €70. The clinician guides your head through a series of positions meant to move the crystals back to where they belong. Clearing may be quick, or it may take another look, because more than one canal can be involved, or because a second condition is present as well. We do not tell you which of those you are before the test.

If the history is mixed — a fall as well as a spin, unsteadiness in crowds, or symptoms that have lasted more than 6 months — we start with the full first assessment rather than a repositioning visit on its own. The assessment costs €145. It includes the gaze test, the positional test and the balance-platform test. We add the walking and turning test when we need to see you move in the corridor, with a handrail there if you need to pause. You and the clinician then agree a plan. A typical plan is 6 sessions over 8–12 weeks, with daily home exercises. A rehabilitation session is 45 minutes and costs €85. A prepaid block of six retraining sessions is €460.

Mara's course can be told because she agreed to it. She was 64. Rolling over set off a spin, and she fell at a tram stop. Her care was a repositioning visit plus 6 sessions over 12 weeks, with 2 short home exercises a day. She got back to walking to the market. Outcomes differ from person to person. Her weeks are not a forecast for yours.

Some dizziness still belongs in an emergency department, not on our list. Go there, or call your local emergency number, if it comes with chest pain, fainting, a sudden severe headache, double vision, a face that has dropped, trouble speaking, or weakness in an arm or a leg. Go there too if it follows a significant head injury and is getting worse. The clinic phone, +1 (555) 014-2200, is for appointments. It is not an emergency line. We are open Monday to Friday 08:00–18:30 and Saturday 08:30–13:00, and closed on Sunday and public holidays.

To book, call that number or write to desk@taira-clinic.example with the subject First assessment request. First appointments are usually within 5 working days. The clinic is at 14 Linden Row, Harbourside, Northgate. Say how long the spinning has lasted, whether a doctor has referred you, and whether rolling over is the main trigger or one of several. An uncertain history is more useful to us than a tidy one.

posts.title: Three things to bring to your first assessment
posts.excerpt: A list of medicines, the shoes you actually walk in, and a note of when the symptom started. The assessment is 60 minutes.
posts.content:
A list of medicines, the shoes you actually walk in, and a note of when the symptom started. The assessment is 60 minutes; you do not need to fast or to stop your usual day.

Sofia Marchetti, our patient coordinator, can answer questions about the visit on +1 (555) 014-2200.

posts.title: Screens, aisles and visual vertigo
posts.excerpt: Supermarket rows, scrolling pages and patterned floors can start a visual vertigo that rest on the sofa does not touch.
posts.content:
Supermarket rows, scrolling pages and patterned floors can start a visual vertigo that rest on the sofa does not touch. Graded exposure, with a clinician, is the usual way back.

Ines, 47, went from avoiding the shop to shopping with a list again. Outcomes differ from person to person.
